title: Lipid Metabolism
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Lipid metabolism links dietary fat, hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and peripheral utilization. Understanding its regulation helps diagnose dyslipidaemia, assess cardiovascular risk and manage complications in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Fats are absorbed as chylomicrons, travel via lymph to blood, and are processed by lipases. The liver repackages fatty acids into VLDL, which matures to IDL and LDL, while HDL returns cholesterol to liver.
b: VLDL → IDL → LDL (delivery of peripheral cholesterol)

sections.p: Triglycerides are hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) at capillary beds, releasing free fatty acids for energy or storage. Hepatic synthesis of VLDL is driven by excess carbohydrate, insulin, and low albumin.
b: LPL activity requires heparan sulphate on endothelium
ApoB-100 is essential for VLDL/LDL assembly
ApoA‑I is the main protein of HDL

sections.p: Hormones and nutritional status fine‑tune lipoprotein production and clearance. Insulin suppresses VLDL, glucagon stimulates hepatic lipolysis, and thyroid hormone increases LDL receptor expression.
Genetic or acquired disturbances alter lipoprotein levels, leading to atherogenic dyslipidaemia, pancreatitis, or fatty liver disease.
b: Secondary causes: HIV protease inhibitors, TB treatment (rifampicin), malaria, chronic hepatitis B, malnutrition

sections.p: Abnormal lipid profiles predict cardiovascular events and guide therapy. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside assessment and simple labs replace sophisticated imaging.
b: Low HDL‑C (< 40 mg/dL men, < 50 mg/dL women) → poor prognosis

t.b: What is the patient’s atherogenic risk? – High LDL‑C or TG directs statin or fibrate therapy
Is acute pancreatitis present? – Elevated enzymes with TG ≥ 500 mg/dL suggest hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis
Provides rapid LDL‑C estimate for urgent risk stratification

sections.p: Focus on interpreting lipid panels, recognising secondary causes, and selecting appropriate first‑line drugs while considering local drug availability and interactions.
b: Statins are first‑line for LDL‑C ≥ 130 mg/dL; avoid in active liver disease
Fibrates treat TG ≥ 500 mg/dL; caution with renal impairment
Niacin rarely used in low‑resource settings due to flushing and hepatotoxicity

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with TG ≥ 500 mg/dL (possible pancreatitis)
Sudden chest pain with LDL‑C ≥ 190 mg/dL and signs of acute coronary syndrome
Rapidly falling albumin with ascites suggesting decompensated liver disease

faq.a: Low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure, stimulating hepatic VLDL synthesis, which later becomes LDL.
Acute malaria often lowers HDL‑C and raises triglycerides due to cytokine‑mediated hepatic changes.

faq.q: When is a lipid panel not reliable?
faq.a: During acute infection, fasting may be impossible, and triglycerides can be falsely high; repeat after recovery.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV on protease inhibitors presents with LDL‑C 160 mg/dL – which drug class is first‑line and why? — Statin; it directly lowers LDL‑C and reduces ASCVD risk, despite drug‑interaction monitoring.

A patient with severe malnutrition has low albumin and LDL‑C 140 mg/dL – what does this indicate about his lipid metabolism? — Hypoalbuminaemia drives hepatic VLDL overproduction, raising LDL‑C despite poor intake.

You receive a lipid panel: LDL‑C 190 mg/dL, HDL‑C 35 mg/dL, TG 180 mg/dL. What is the next step in a district hospital without imaging? — Start high‑intensity statin, assess for secondary causes, and arrange follow‑up lipid repeat in 4‑6 weeks.

A patient on rifampicin for TB develops TG 620 mg/dL and abdominal pain – what is the likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis; stop offending drug if possible, start IV fluids, analgesia, and consider fibrate if available.
How does glucagon affect lipid metabolism during fasting? — It stimulates hepatic lipolysis, increasing free fatty acids for ketogenesis and modestly raising VLDL output.
Which genetic disorder presents with tendon xanthomas and markedly high LDL‑C in a young adult? — Familial hypercholesterolaemia; LDL‑C often > 190 mg/dL, requires early statin therapy.

In a patient with chronic hepatitis B, you note low HDL‑C and high TG – what is the clinical significance? — Dyslipidaemia contributes to accelerated atherosclerosis; monitor cardiovascular risk and consider lifestyle modification.
Why are fibrates avoided in patients with chronic kidney disease? — They are renally excreted and can precipitate rhabdomyolysis in reduced renal clearance.
